evaluated.name: Issuance purged book-to-market
evaluated.expression: RATIO(SUB(ceq, TS_SUM(SUB(sstk, prstkc), 3)), MUL(prcc_f, csho))
evaluated.hypothesis: Book equity accumulated by recently selling shares is not evidence of cheapness; only book equity retained or repurchased against reflects real value, so removing three years of cumulative net equity issuance from the numerator sharpens the value signal.
evaluated.reasoning: This embeds financing directly inside the valuation ratio instead of adding a second sorting leg, mechanically penalizing serial issuers whose high B/M is an artifact of paid-in capital and rewarding repurchasers whose book has been depleted by cash returned to owners. The three-year window captures the persistence of financing policy while keeping coverage close to that of plain book-to-market.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cash flow yield times deleveraging
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(oancf, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(dltr, dltis), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A high operating cash-flow yield is credible undervaluation when the firm is using that cash to retire debt; a low cash-flow yield combined with heavy new debt issuance signals a richly priced firm sustaining itself with borrowed capital.
evaluated.reasoning: This routes the financing channel through debt rather than equity, so it is a mechanically distinct source of information from buyback-based signals and avoids the option-grant noise in sstk. Net debt retirement is a costly, verifiable commitment that corroborates the cash-generating capacity implied by the valuation ratio, so the joint-extreme cells should carry the FF5 alpha.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Buyback value accretion per share
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(MUL(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: The wealth transferred to continuing shareholders by a share transaction is the product of the fraction of the float transacted and the gap between fundamental value and price, so net repurchases executed at a deep discount to book accrete value per remaining share, while equity issued at a discount to book dilutes it and equity issued at a premium is largely neutral.
evaluated.reasoning: This is not a rank blend of book-to-market and net payout: the two legs are multiplied because the accretion mechanism is literally a product, and the resulting cross-section is asymmetric in a way neither published anomaly produces — the most negative scores are cheap firms diluting shareholders (constrained issuers selling assets below book), not merely expensive issuers. Both legs share the same market-cap denominator so the product has clean units of book value acquired per dollar of market value, and the 1% symmetric winsorization keeps microcap firms with tiny market caps from dominating the tails.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Repurchase timed to own valuation trough
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), TS_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 5))
evaluated.hypothesis: Managers hold private information about their own firm's intrinsic value, so the informative event is buying back stock when the firm's valuation is depressed relative to its own five-year history, and issuing stock when its own valuation is at a multi-year peak; cross-sectional cheapness is not required for this timing signal to carry information.
evaluated.reasoning: The valuation leg is a within-firm time-series percentile rather than a cross-sectional value score, so this cannot be a re-labeling of book-to-market and avoids the sector- and business-model-driven level differences that make cross-sectional value traps, and it sidesteps the negative-enterprise-value denominator problem entirely. Both legs are bounded on [0,1] and the product is monotone increasing in each, concentrating longs in firms repurchasing heavily at their own valuation trough and shorts in firms issuing heavily at their own valuation peak — a pure managerial-timing interaction that neither leg identifies alone.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Levered buyback conviction conditioned on price
evaluated.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)), RANK(MIN(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), at), RATIO(SUB(dltis, dltr), at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm that simultaneously raises debt and retires equity is making a leveraged, irreversible bet on its own share price, so the value effect should be much steeper within this group: cheap debt-for-equity swappers are high-conviction undervaluation, while expensive firms levering up to buy back stock are destroying value through financial engineering.
evaluated.reasoning: The MIN operator makes the conditioning variable positive only when both financing legs point the same way (debt in, equity out), which is a joint financing state that neither net equity issuance nor net debt issuance identifies separately, so this is not a differenced pair of published anomalies. The financing leg enters as a bounded [0,1] rank weight and the valuation leg as a centered z-score, so the signal is a genuine varying-slope interaction — value information is switched on for swappers and attenuated toward zero for everyone else — rather than the discontinuous splice of two incomparable rank scales the critic identified.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Sales yield confirmed by dividend commitment
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(revt, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(dvt, at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Sales-to-price identifies firms whose revenue base is cheaply priced but says nothing about whether the cash is real; a contemporaneous increase in total dividends is a costly, sticky commitment that management makes only when it believes the depressed valuation understates sustainable cash generation.
evaluated.reasoning: Dividends (dvt) have near-complete coverage back to the 1950s and dividend changes are far less mechanically correlated with book equity than buybacks are, so this leg should add information that HML cannot absorb, addressing the alpha-versus-slope divergence rather than restating it. Sales-to-price is chosen over book-to-market precisely because it is the value proxy least collinear with HML's book-based construction, and the change (rather than level) of dividend intensity keeps the signal from degenerating into a stale payer/non-payer dummy.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Industry neutral cheap repurchaser
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), MUL(prcc_f, csho))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Both cheapness and buyback intensity are strongly sector-determined, so the informative comparison is within industry: a firm cheap relative to its own peers that is also retiring more equity than its peers is revealing firm-specific undervaluation rather than sector-level pricing.
evaluated.reasoning: The generation-0 buyback-value signals had solid FMB t-stats but zero FF5 alpha, consistent with the long-short spread being a sector value tilt that HML and CMA already price; industry-relative ranking on both legs strips exactly that component and leaves the idiosyncratic managerial-information component. It isolates a single design choice — neutralization — against the accepted archive members, so a positive result cleanly attributes the alpha gap to sector spanning rather than to the mechanism itself.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Financing policy reversal at cheap prices
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Buyback and issuance levels are highly persistent and therefore largely anticipated, so the surprise lies in the transition — a firm that swings from net issuer to net repurchaser while trading at a high earnings yield is delivering new information about management's view of its own price.
evaluated.reasoning: Every archive signal used the level of the financing state; this isolates the change, which is the natural candidate for unpriced information and for a spread that FF5 factors (built from slow-moving level characteristics) cannot span. If the change-based version delivers alpha where the level-based versions did not, that identifies staleness — not sample or scaling — as the binding constraint on the whole family.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Discounted cash released by payout
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(che, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(dvt, che), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The market applies a deep discount to cash it believes will be hoarded or wasted, so a firm whose cash balance is large relative to its market capitalization is mispriced only if management is actually releasing that cash to owners; the payout rate out of the cash stock is the catalyst that converts a balance-sheet discount into realized return.
evaluated.reasoning: This abandons the leverage/deleveraging channel entirely and prices a different asset — the cash stock itself — so it is not a variable substitution on the archived cash-flow-yield-times-deleveraging bet, and the agency mechanism (trapped cash discount released by distribution) is specific to the pairing rather than to either leg alone. Cash-to-price alone is a distress-tilted, HML-correlated value proxy and the payout rate out of cash alone is a maturity proxy, but their joint tail — cheap cash that is verifiably being distributed — is the agency-discount-closing cell, and both che and dvt are populated across essentially the full panel so the portfolios stay wide.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Buyback conviction inside the glamour segment
evaluated.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)), INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ceq)), 0.7))
evaluated.hypothesis: Among cheap firms, repurchasing is the expected and largely anticipated action; the genuinely informative event is a richly valued firm that retires equity anyway, which separates growth firms with real cash generation from those whose high multiple rests on continual dilution.
evaluated.reasoning: Both the long and short legs are drawn from the same top-30% market-to-book segment, so unlike the flagged rank difference the spread carries no mechanical loading on book-to-market in either direction — a null result is then interpretable as "financing conveys nothing within glamour" rather than being confounded by a deliberately short value tilt. Firms outside the gate score exactly zero and sit in the middle of the cross-section, so the sort's extremes are populated only by expensive repurchasers versus expensive diluters, which is precisely the conditional claim being tested.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Earnings covered dividend yield
evaluated.expression: RATIO(MIN(dvt, ib), MUL(prcc_f, csho))
evaluated.hypothesis: A high dividend yield is evidence of undervaluation only to the extent the payout is funded by current earnings; the portion of a distribution that exceeds earnings is a liquidation or a soon-to-be-cut promise, so capping the payout at earnings before scaling by price separates sustainable yield from doomed yield.
evaluated.reasoning: The MIN operator makes the valuation and financing legs interact inside a single ratio rather than through the ZSCORE-times-RANK gate architecture that has now failed twice, and it produces an economically different quantity from either dividend yield or earnings yield: firms paying out more than they earn are pushed down to their earnings yield, and loss-making payers are pushed negative into the short leg. Coverage rests on dvt, ib and prcc_f, all populated across the full panel for dividend payers, giving a wide and stable sort that neither the buyback-based nor cash-flow-statement-based archive signals could support.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Payout instrument tilted to buybacks when cheap
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, dvt), ADD(prstkc, dvt))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Conditional on returning capital at all, the *choice* of instrument reveals management's price view: repurchases are the value-accretive instrument only when the stock is cheap, so a cheap firm that skews its payout mix toward buybacks rather than dividends is making a price-contingent capital allocation decision that a dividend-paying peer is not.
evaluated.reasoning: This holds total payout roughly fixed and varies only its composition, so unlike every archive signal it is not a payout-yield or net-issuance bet and should carry little RMW or HML loading — the mechanism is capital allocation skill conditional on price, not the amount of cash returned. The mix ratio is bounded in [−1,1] by construction, which keeps the rank well behaved, and the interaction is essential: a buyback-tilted mix at a high price is value destruction, so neither leg carries the hypothesis alone.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cheapness with stable financing policy
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(NEG(VOL(RATIO(SUB(sstk, prstkc), at), 5))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Erratic swings between raising and returning equity capital indicate a firm whose funding is dictated by external conditions rather than by a considered view of value; a cheap firm with a quiet, stable financing record is more likely mispriced, while a cheap firm with volatile financing is capital-constrained and correctly discounted.
evaluated.reasoning: Every archive signal uses the first moment of financing (a level or a change); this is the first to use its second moment, which is a distinguishable economic construct — funding fragility — rather than a rescaling of net issuance. It also offers a direct contrast with the accepted financing-reversal signal: if large *changes* in policy are informative but high *volatility* of policy is harmful, that jointly identifies deliberate reversal, not noise, as the source of the alpha.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Serial repurchaser at a cash flow discount
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(oancf, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), TS_SUM(INDICATOR(SUB(prstkc, sstk), 0), 5))
evaluated.hypothesis: A single year of net repurchase is often mechanical (option-plan offsets, one-off tenders), whereas repeating the decision in most of the past five years is a revealed, persistent judgment that the shares are undervalued; combined with a high operating cash-flow yield this identifies firms whose price ignores a durable, self-funded distribution policy.
evaluated.reasoning: The count of repurchase years is a persistence measure that is nearly uncorrelated with repurchase intensity, so it separates conviction from magnitude — a distinction none of the archive's level, change, or timing constructions can make. Using operating cash flow rather than earnings in the valuation leg avoids the accrual-driven E/P tail and keeps the long leg out of the deep-value bucket that generated the negative alpha in generation 1.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Hoard liquidation at a cash discount
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(che, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(dvt, prstkc), oancf), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The agency discount on corporate cash closes only when the hoard itself is being drawn down, so the informative firm is one whose market price already reflects a deep discount on its liquid assets *and* whose distributions exceed what current operations generate — payout financed from the balance sheet rather than from the income statement.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the unstable dvt/che denominator (which explodes for low-cash payers and plausibly drives the archive's FMB-versus-alpha gap) with distributions net of operating cash flow scaled by assets, a bounded quantity whose sign has direct economic meaning. It also changes the economics rather than the normalization: routine dividend payers funding payout from earnings score near zero, and only firms actively converting the discounted hoard into shareholder cash reach the long leg, which is the specific event the agency story says should be repriced.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Dividend initiation versus omission when cheap
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), SUB(INDICATOR(dvt, 0), INDICATOR(LAG(dvt, 1), 0)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Among cheaply priced firms, the discrete decision to start paying a dividend is a costly, hard-to-reverse confirmation that the depressed price understates sustainable cash flow, whereas the decision to stop paying confirms that the low price is a solvency assessment — so valuation carries genuinely opposite information across the two events.
evaluated.reasoning: The financing leg takes values +1, 0, −1 for initiators, unchanged-status firms and omitters, so the long leg is cheap initiators and the short leg is cheap omitters — this actually tests the regime reversal that earlier conditional proposals only claimed, and it is a discrete corporate event rather than another continuous flow rescaling. Payment-status changes are not a characteristic FF5 factors are built from, dvt has near-complete panel coverage, and the design is orthogonal to the archived buyback family both in variable and in event type.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Raising equity while paying it back out
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), revt)), IND_RANK(MIN(RATIO(sstk, at), RATIO(dvt, at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm that simultaneously sells new shares and distributes cash to existing holders is round-tripping capital at a cost; when it does so from a rich price-to-sales multiple, the issuance is opportunistic use of overvalued currency and the dividend is a signaling expense, so subsequent returns should be low.
evaluated.reasoning: The MIN operator identifies simultaneity — a state neither net external financing nor gross issuance can express, since netting these flows makes a raise-and-distribute firm look financially neutral — so this is not the XFIN anomaly relabeled, and it avoids gross dltis entirely and with it the revolver-rollover contamination. The financing leg is industry-ranked to prevent the signal from collapsing into a REIT and utility bet, where mandatory distribution plus continuous equity issuance is structural rather than informative, and the rich-multiple leg is on the short side where generation 1's negative sales-yield alpha says the price-multiple return actually lives.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Persistent payout mix when cheap
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(SUB(prstkc, dvt), 3), TS_SUM(ADD(prstkc, dvt), 3))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The instrument-choice signal reflects a standing capital-allocation policy rather than a single year's tender offer, so measuring the buyback-versus-dividend tilt over three years of cumulative payout captures the persistent managerial view of price while filtering out one-off transactions and years of accidental zero payout.
evaluated.reasoning: A three-year cumulation defines the mix for any firm that paid out at all in the window, which should lift coverage above the 0.079 of the single-year version and stabilize decile membership month to month — the two diagnostics most likely to be limiting the winner's alpha t-stat. It isolates a single design choice (measurement horizon of the composition variable) against the archive's best result, so the contrast is directly interpretable as noise-versus-signal in the mix leg.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Sector relative payout mix when cheap
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, dvt), ADD(prstkc, dvt))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Payout instrument norms are set at the industry level — utilities and staples distribute through dividends by convention while technology and healthcare distribute through repurchases — so the price-contingent decision is a firm's deviation from its own sector's payout convention, not its position in the pooled cross-section.
evaluated.reasoning: The pooled mix rank almost certainly contains a large static sector component that adds noise to the interaction and drags the long leg toward whole industries; ranking the mix within industry strips that component and leaves the firm-specific instrument choice the hypothesis is about. This isolates neutralization as the single varied design element against the archive's strongest result, and neutralization has already been shown to move alpha from negative to positive for the cheap-repurchaser family.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Buyback over dividend intensity when cheap
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, dvt), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: If the instrument-choice effect is genuine, it should survive being expressed as a signed intensity — buyback dollars in excess of dividend dollars scaled by assets — which also assigns non-payers a well-defined score of zero rather than dropping them.
evaluated.reasoning: This discriminates between two very different readings of the archive's best result: a pure composition effect (bounded ratio, payers only) versus a signed magnitude effect (unbounded intensity, whole cross-section). If the intensity version reproduces the alpha, the mechanism is robust and coverage nearly doubles; if it collapses, we learn that the information is specifically in the *choice conditional on paying out*, which sharpens every subsequent refinement.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Equity versus debt retirement when cheap
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, dltr), ADD(prstkc, dltr))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm with cash to return faces a relative-value decision between retiring its own equity and retiring its own debt; choosing equity while the stock trades at a high earnings yield reveals that management judges its equity to be the cheaper claim to repurchase, whereas paying down debt at the same price reveals the opposite.
evaluated.reasoning: This applies the instrument-choice logic that worked to an entirely different decision margin — across the capital structure rather than between two forms of shareholder payout — so it tests whether the mechanism is "management picks the mispriced claim" or narrowly "buybacks beat dividends." Both components are uses of cash rather than a use versus a source, so the ratio is bounded and interpretable, and the cell is disjoint from the dividend-mix cell, giving genuinely incremental evidence rather than a rescaling.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Pecking order choice at a discount
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(dltis, sstk), ADD(dltis, sstk))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Among firms that must raise capital, the choice of instrument is the informative variable: a cheaply priced firm that funds itself with debt rather than by selling shares is refusing to issue equity it considers undervalued, while a cheaply priced firm that sells equity anyway is either constrained or aware that the discount is deserved.
evaluated.reasoning: This extends instrument choice to the capital-raising side, where the archive has only ever tested net or gross amounts, and it populates a completely different set of firms — issuers rather than payers — so it can raise the coverage of the mechanism family beyond the payer subsample without diluting the economics. The bounded raise-mix ratio also neutralizes firm size and financing scale, keeping the sort from degenerating into the published net-issuance anomaly.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Pure interaction of price and payout instrument
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, dvt), ADD(prstkc, dvt))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The correct instrument depends on price: retiring shares creates value when the stock is cheap and destroys it when the stock is rich, while a dividend is the neutral instrument at any price, so returns should be high for cheap buyback-tilted firms and for expensive dividend-tilted firms and low for the two mismatched cells.
evaluated.reasoning: Multiplying two demeaned variables produces the interaction term itself, which is approximately orthogonal to both main effects, so unlike the flagged gated version there is no mass of exact zeros, no truncated cross-section, and no residual loading on either the value premium or the payout-composition premium — a positive alpha here cannot be explained by either single-theme anomaly. This is the decisive test of whether the archive's best result is a genuine conditional mechanism or merely two additive effects riding in the same rank product, and it uses the entire payer cross-section on both sides rather than 30% of it.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Payout mix with neutral non payers
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(COALESCE(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, dvt), ADD(prstkc, dvt)), RATIO(SUB(prstkc, dvt), at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm that distributes nothing has made no instrument choice and should be scored neutrally rather than dropped, so the payout-mix signal should extend to the full cross-section with non-payers placed between the dividend-only and buyback-only extremes.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive's best signal discards roughly a third of otherwise usable firm-months purely because 0/0 is undefined, and that thin, payer-only cross-section is the most likely cap on its alpha t-stat and portfolio stability. The COALESCE convention is economically justified rather than a coverage patch: when total payout is zero the fallback evaluates to exactly zero, which is precisely the neutral midpoint of the [−1, 1] mix scale, so the ordering of genuine payers is untouched while non-choosers occupy the middle.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Shift toward buybacks when cheap
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, dvt), ADD(prstkc, dvt)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The informative act is the moment management re-weights its payout toward repurchases while the stock is cheap; a firm that has always bought back stock is executing a standing policy, whereas one that swings its mix this year is responding to a price it now considers too low.
evaluated.reasoning: This separates the state from the shift within the winning mechanism — an open question the archive cannot answer, since the level-based mix and the level-based net-issuance signals were tested but only net *issuance* was ever differenced. If the change version retains most of the alpha, the effect is news-driven and should be traded at higher frequency; if it collapses, the effect is a stable policy characteristic and the three-year smoothed version is the right consolidation target.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Payout mix at a composite discount
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, dvt), ADD(prstkc, dvt))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Whether a repurchase is value-accretive depends on true undervaluation, which a single accounting multiple measures with error — loss-makers and firms with transitory earnings are misclassified by E/P alone — so a two-multiple price signal should sharpen the same interaction.
evaluated.reasoning: Every instrument-choice test so far has held the valuation leg fixed at industry-ranked E/P, leaving unexamined whether the mechanism is limited by noise in the price measurement rather than in the financing measurement. Averaging the earnings and book yields before industry-ranking reduces that measurement error without changing the economic claim, and it directly addresses the negative-alpha lesson from generation 1 by keeping the price leg from being a single deep-multiple extreme.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Committed buyback tilt when cheap
evaluated.expression: MUL(MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, dvt), ADD(prstkc, dvt)))), RANK(RATIO(ADD(prstkc, dvt), MUL(prcc_f, csho))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Composition reveals the direction of management's price view and total payout yield reveals how much capital is behind it, so the strongest undervaluation evidence is a cheap firm that returns a large fraction of its market value and chooses to do so through repurchases.
evaluated.reasoning: The mix ratio deliberately discards magnitude, and the separate intensity test (alpha 4.2%, t=3.36) showed magnitude carries independent information, so the open question is whether the two are complementary or substitutes — a three-way rank product answers it directly. If the triple interaction beats both two-way versions, the long leg should be restricted to high-conviction, well-funded repurchasers, which is also the cell least likely to be arbitraged away by mechanical option-offset buybacks.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Payout mix against own price history
evaluated.expression: MUL(TS_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 5), RANK(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, dvt), ADD(prstkc, dvt))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The price that should govern the buyback-versus-dividend decision is the firm's own valuation relative to its history, not its rank against unrelated firms; a company tilting to repurchases while its own book-to-market sits at a five-year high is buying at its own trough.
evaluated.reasoning: This substitutes a within-firm price benchmark for the cross-sectional one and thereby distinguishes two very different readings of the winning result — cross-sectional value premium amplification versus genuine managerial market timing — which no archive signal has separated, since the earlier own-history test paired the trough with net repurchase *intensity* rather than with instrument choice. A within-firm benchmark also carries almost no HML loading, so a comparable alpha here would show the mechanism does not depend on riding the value factor.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Share of internal cash flow distributed when cheap
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(MUL(INDICATOR(oancf, 0), WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(prstkc, dvt), oancf), 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The prior decision to the instrument choice is what fraction of self-generated cash a firm hands back rather than retains; a cheaply priced firm that returns a large share of genuinely positive operating cash flow is resolving the agency discount on retained funds, while one that keeps it confirms the discount.
evaluated.reasoning: Routing the retention decision through operating cash flow rather than the change in the cash balance removes the flaw the critic identified — a firm burning cash to fund losses or capex now has no way to reach the long leg, because the INDICATOR gate zeroes out every firm with non-positive operating cash flow and the numerator counts only actual distributions rather than any decline in the cash stock. The construction keeps the scale-free, bounded character that made payout composition work, uses a 1% winsorization to stop balance-sheet-funded overdistribution from dominating the tail, and tests the retain-versus-release margin that the archive's instrument-choice results have never isolated.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Composite discount with full sample mix
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), RANK(COALESCE(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, dvt), ADD(prstkc, dvt)), RATIO(SUB(prstkc, dvt), at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The instrument-choice interaction should hold on the full cross-section, with firms that distribute nothing scored at the neutral midpoint rather than excluded, so the stronger price leg and the wider sample should reinforce each other.
evaluated.reasoning: Coverage is the champion's one weak diagnostic (0.079), and the neutral-non-payer convention already demonstrated that widening to 0.121 costs only about one point of alpha when paired with the weaker single-multiple value leg. Pairing the wide sample with the better price measurement tests directly whether the alpha decay came from the extra firms or from noise in the E/P leg, which determines whether the deployable version of this mechanism is payer-only or universal.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Normalized firm yield with rebalanced residual
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(MA(ebitda, 3), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)))), RANK(SUB(RANK(COALESCE(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, dvt), ADD(prstkc, dvt)), SIGN(SUB(prstkc, dvt)))), SUMRANK(VOL(RATIO(ib, at), 5), TS_SUM(INDICATOR(dvt, 0), 5)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Management compares its share price against normal earning power rather than a single year's operating result, so a three-year averaged enterprise yield is the discount measure that best identifies genuinely undervalued repurchasers, especially at cyclical troughs.
evaluated.reasoning: The cyclically adjusted enterprise yield produced the archive's best Sharpe (0.580) and a strong slope (6.67) when paired with the raw wide mix, so pairing it with the purged, re-ranked financing leg tests whether the time-series normalization of the price leg and the motive-purging of the financing leg are complementary. It also directly addresses the risk that earnings-volatility purging tilts the sample toward stable firms while a single-year EBITDA misprices the cyclical ones that remain.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Two year stance discretion residual
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)))), RANK(SUB(RANK(COALESCE(RATIO(TS_SUM(SUB(prstkc, dvt), 2), TS_SUM(ADD(prstkc, dvt), 2)), SIGN(SUB(prstkc, dvt)))), SUMRANK(VOL(RATIO(ib, at), 5), TS_SUM(INDICATOR(dvt, 0), 5)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Management's price-contingent instrument choice is best read over the last two years of cumulative distributions, which captures both the standing stance and the allocation of recently generated cash while averaging out the lumpiness of a single tender offer.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the five-term fusion of two separate financing legs with a single, interpretable measurement change — the window over which the payout composition is cumulated — so the result is attributable against the accepted one-year version by exactly one knob. It also makes no coverage promise it cannot keep: the two-year cumulation is subsumed by the five-year purge terms that already bind, and cumulating over two years rather than one strictly reduces the 0/0 cases that the SIGN fallback must handle, while the three-year version of this same cumulation previously delivered the best Sharpe of its generation.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Current state discretion residual
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)))), RANK(SUB(RANK(COALESCE(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, dvt), ADD(prstkc, dvt)), SIGN(SUB(prstkc, dvt)))), SUMRANK(VOL(RATIO(ib, at), 3), RATIO(dvt, at)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The two motives that mechanically shape payout composition are both current-state properties — how unstable recent earnings are and how large a dividend the firm is currently carrying — so neither requires a five-year history to measure, and purging on contemporaneous quantities should isolate the same discretionary residual on a much larger sample.
evaluated.reasoning: The previous version was internally inconsistent because the binding history requirement was the five-year dividend-payer count, not the volatility window; replacing that count with the current dividend-to-assets ratio removes the long-history constraint from both purge terms at once, so the coverage argument now actually follows from the expression. It is also an economic improvement rather than a lookback tweak: a continuous measure of the dividend a firm is presently carrying describes its commitment far better than counting how many of the last five years it paid anything, and the graded-commitment purge already raised the cross-sectional slope from 5.11 to 5.92 when tested at a three-year horizon.
evaluated.author: proposer

considered.name: Earnings yield times float shrinkage
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(NEG(GROWTH(csho, 1))))
considered.hypothesis: The undervaluation revealed by a high earnings yield is strongest when the share count is actually contracting, and overvaluation is most severe when a low-earnings-yield firm is simultaneously expanding its share count.
considered.reasoning: Both ranks are uniform on [0,1], so the product is monotone increasing in each leg but superadditive at the joint extremes, concentrating long positions in cheap repurchasers and short positions in expensive issuers rather than in mid-cell firms. Share-count change is a cleaner, higher-coverage measure of true net equity financing than sstk/prstkc dollar flows because it nets out option exercises, M&A stock, and secondary offerings.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Issuance purged book-to-market
considered.expression: RATIO(SUB(ceq, TS_SUM(SUB(sstk, prstkc), 3)), MUL(prcc_f, csho))
considered.hypothesis: Book equity accumulated by recently selling shares is not evidence of cheapness; only book equity retained or repurchased against reflects real value, so removing three years of cumulative net equity issuance from the numerator sharpens the value signal.
considered.reasoning: This embeds financing directly inside the valuation ratio instead of adding a second sorting leg, mechanically penalizing serial issuers whose high B/M is an artifact of paid-in capital and rewarding repurchasers whose book has been depleted by cash returned to owners. The three-year window captures the persistence of financing policy while keeping coverage close to that of plain book-to-market.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cash flow yield times deleveraging
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(oancf, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(dltr, dltis), at)))
considered.hypothesis: A high operating cash-flow yield is credible undervaluation when the firm is using that cash to retire debt; a low cash-flow yield combined with heavy new debt issuance signals a richly priced firm sustaining itself with borrowed capital.
considered.reasoning: This routes the financing channel through debt rather than equity, so it is a mechanically distinct source of information from buyback-based signals and avoids the option-grant noise in sstk. Net debt retirement is a costly, verifiable commitment that corroborates the cash-generating capacity implied by the valuation ratio, so the joint-extreme cells should carry the FF5 alpha.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Buyback value accretion per share
considered.expression: WINSOR(MUL(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 1)
considered.hypothesis: The wealth transferred to continuing shareholders by a share transaction is the product of the fraction of the float transacted and the gap between fundamental value and price, so net repurchases executed at a deep discount to book accrete value per remaining share, while equity issued at a discount to book dilutes it and equity issued at a premium is largely neutral.
considered.reasoning: This is not a rank blend of book-to-market and net payout: the two legs are multiplied because the accretion mechanism is literally a product, and the resulting cross-section is asymmetric in a way neither published anomaly produces — the most negative scores are cheap firms diluting shareholders (constrained issuers selling assets below book), not merely expensive issuers. Both legs share the same market-cap denominator so the product has clean units of book value acquired per dollar of market value, and the 1% symmetric winsorization keeps microcap firms with tiny market caps from dominating the tails.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Repurchase timed to own valuation trough
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), TS_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 5))
considered.hypothesis: Managers hold private information about their own firm's intrinsic value, so the informative event is buying back stock when the firm's valuation is depressed relative to its own five-year history, and issuing stock when its own valuation is at a multi-year peak; cross-sectional cheapness is not required for this timing signal to carry information.
considered.reasoning: The valuation leg is a within-firm time-series percentile rather than a cross-sectional value score, so this cannot be a re-labeling of book-to-market and avoids the sector- and business-model-driven level differences that make cross-sectional value traps, and it sidesteps the negative-enterprise-value denominator problem entirely. Both legs are bounded on [0,1] and the product is monotone increasing in each, concentrating longs in firms repurchasing heavily at their own valuation trough and shorts in firms issuing heavily at their own valuation peak — a pure managerial-timing interaction that neither leg identifies alone.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Levered buyback conviction conditioned on price
considered.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)), RANK(MIN(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), at), RATIO(SUB(dltis, dltr), at))))
considered.hypothesis: A firm that simultaneously raises debt and retires equity is making a leveraged, irreversible bet on its own share price, so the value effect should be much steeper within this group: cheap debt-for-equity swappers are high-conviction undervaluation, while expensive firms levering up to buy back stock are destroying value through financial engineering.
considered.reasoning: The MIN operator makes the conditioning variable positive only when both financing legs point the same way (debt in, equity out), which is a joint financing state that neither net equity issuance nor net debt issuance identifies separately, so this is not a differenced pair of published anomalies. The financing leg enters as a bounded [0,1] rank weight and the valuation leg as a centered z-score, so the signal is a genuine varying-slope interaction — value information is switched on for swappers and attenuated toward zero for everyone else — rather than the discontinuous splice of two incomparable rank scales the critic identified.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Sales yield confirmed by dividend commitment
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(revt, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(dvt, at), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Sales-to-price identifies firms whose revenue base is cheaply priced but says nothing about whether the cash is real; a contemporaneous increase in total dividends is a costly, sticky commitment that management makes only when it believes the depressed valuation understates sustainable cash generation.
considered.reasoning: Dividends (dvt) have near-complete coverage back to the 1950s and dividend changes are far less mechanically correlated with book equity than buybacks are, so this leg should add information that HML cannot absorb, addressing the alpha-versus-slope divergence rather than restating it. Sales-to-price is chosen over book-to-market precisely because it is the value proxy least collinear with HML's book-based construction, and the change (rather than level) of dividend intensity keeps the signal from degenerating into a stale payer/non-payer dummy.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Industry neutral cheap repurchaser
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), MUL(prcc_f, csho))))
considered.hypothesis: Both cheapness and buyback intensity are strongly sector-determined, so the informative comparison is within industry: a firm cheap relative to its own peers that is also retiring more equity than its peers is revealing firm-specific undervaluation rather than sector-level pricing.
considered.reasoning: The generation-0 buyback-value signals had solid FMB t-stats but zero FF5 alpha, consistent with the long-short spread being a sector value tilt that HML and CMA already price; industry-relative ranking on both legs strips exactly that component and leaves the idiosyncratic managerial-information component. It isolates a single design choice — neutralization — against the accepted archive members, so a positive result cleanly attributes the alpha gap to sector spanning rather than to the mechanism itself.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Financing policy reversal at cheap prices
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), at), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Buyback and issuance levels are highly persistent and therefore largely anticipated, so the surprise lies in the transition — a firm that swings from net issuer to net repurchaser while trading at a high earnings yield is delivering new information about management's view of its own price.
considered.reasoning: Every archive signal used the level of the financing state; this isolates the change, which is the natural candidate for unpriced information and for a spread that FF5 factors (built from slow-moving level characteristics) cannot span. If the change-based version delivers alpha where the level-based versions did not, that identifies staleness — not sample or scaling — as the binding constraint on the whole family.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Discounted cash released by payout
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(che, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(dvt, che), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: The market applies a deep discount to cash it believes will be hoarded or wasted, so a firm whose cash balance is large relative to its market capitalization is mispriced only if management is actually releasing that cash to owners; the payout rate out of the cash stock is the catalyst that converts a balance-sheet discount into realized return.
considered.reasoning: This abandons the leverage/deleveraging channel entirely and prices a different asset — the cash stock itself — so it is not a variable substitution on the archived cash-flow-yield-times-deleveraging bet, and the agency mechanism (trapped cash discount released by distribution) is specific to the pairing rather than to either leg alone. Cash-to-price alone is a distress-tilted, HML-correlated value proxy and the payout rate out of cash alone is a maturity proxy, but their joint tail — cheap cash that is verifiably being distributed — is the agency-discount-closing cell, and both che and dvt are populated across essentially the full panel so the portfolios stay wide.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Buyback conviction inside the glamour segment
considered.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)), INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ceq)), 0.7))
considered.hypothesis: Among cheap firms, repurchasing is the expected and largely anticipated action; the genuinely informative event is a richly valued firm that retires equity anyway, which separates growth firms with real cash generation from those whose high multiple rests on continual dilution.
considered.reasoning: Both the long and short legs are drawn from the same top-30% market-to-book segment, so unlike the flagged rank difference the spread carries no mechanical loading on book-to-market in either direction — a null result is then interpretable as "financing conveys nothing within glamour" rather than being confounded by a deliberately short value tilt. Firms outside the gate score exactly zero and sit in the middle of the cross-section, so the sort's extremes are populated only by expensive repurchasers versus expensive diluters, which is precisely the conditional claim being tested.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Earnings covered dividend yield
considered.expression: RATIO(MIN(dvt, ib), MUL(prcc_f, csho))
considered.hypothesis: A high dividend yield is evidence of undervaluation only to the extent the payout is funded by current earnings; the portion of a distribution that exceeds earnings is a liquidation or a soon-to-be-cut promise, so capping the payout at earnings before scaling by price separates sustainable yield from doomed yield.
considered.reasoning: The MIN operator makes the valuation and financing legs interact inside a single ratio rather than through the ZSCORE-times-RANK gate architecture that has now failed twice, and it produces an economically different quantity from either dividend yield or earnings yield: firms paying out more than they earn are pushed down to their earnings yield, and loss-making payers are pushed negative into the short leg. Coverage rests on dvt, ib and prcc_f, all populated across the full panel for dividend payers, giving a wide and stable sort that neither the buyback-based nor cash-flow-statement-based archive signals could support.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Payout instrument tilted to buybacks when cheap
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, dvt), ADD(prstkc, dvt))))
considered.hypothesis: Conditional on returning capital at all, the *choice* of instrument reveals management's price view: repurchases are the value-accretive instrument only when the stock is cheap, so a cheap firm that skews its payout mix toward buybacks rather than dividends is making a price-contingent capital allocation decision that a dividend-paying peer is not.
considered.reasoning: This holds total payout roughly fixed and varies only its composition, so unlike every archive signal it is not a payout-yield or net-issuance bet and should carry little RMW or HML loading — the mechanism is capital allocation skill conditional on price, not the amount of cash returned. The mix ratio is bounded in [−1,1] by construction, which keeps the rank well behaved, and the interaction is essential: a buyback-tilted mix at a high price is value destruction, so neither leg carries the hypothesis alone.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cheapness with stable financing policy
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(NEG(VOL(RATIO(SUB(sstk, prstkc), at), 5))))
considered.hypothesis: Erratic swings between raising and returning equity capital indicate a firm whose funding is dictated by external conditions rather than by a considered view of value; a cheap firm with a quiet, stable financing record is more likely mispriced, while a cheap firm with volatile financing is capital-constrained and correctly discounted.
considered.reasoning: Every archive signal uses the first moment of financing (a level or a change); this is the first to use its second moment, which is a distinguishable economic construct — funding fragility — rather than a rescaling of net issuance. It also offers a direct contrast with the accepted financing-reversal signal: if large *changes* in policy are informative but high *volatility* of policy is harmful, that jointly identifies deliberate reversal, not noise, as the source of the alpha.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Serial repurchaser at a cash flow discount
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(oancf, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), TS_SUM(INDICATOR(SUB(prstkc, sstk), 0), 5))
considered.hypothesis: A single year of net repurchase is often mechanical (option-plan offsets, one-off tenders), whereas repeating the decision in most of the past five years is a revealed, persistent judgment that the shares are undervalued; combined with a high operating cash-flow yield this identifies firms whose price ignores a durable, self-funded distribution policy.
considered.reasoning: The count of repurchase years is a persistence measure that is nearly uncorrelated with repurchase intensity, so it separates conviction from magnitude — a distinction none of the archive's level, change, or timing constructions can make. Using operating cash flow rather than earnings in the valuation leg avoids the accrual-driven E/P tail and keeps the long leg out of the deep-value bucket that generated the negative alpha in generation 1.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Hoard liquidation at a cash discount
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(che, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(dvt, prstkc), oancf), at)))
considered.hypothesis: The agency discount on corporate cash closes only when the hoard itself is being drawn down, so the informative firm is one whose market price already reflects a deep discount on its liquid assets *and* whose distributions exceed what current operations generate — payout financed from the balance sheet rather than from the income statement.
considered.reasoning: This replaces the unstable dvt/che denominator (which explodes for low-cash payers and plausibly drives the archive's FMB-versus-alpha gap) with distributions net of operating cash flow scaled by assets, a bounded quantity whose sign has direct economic meaning. It also changes the economics rather than the normalization: routine dividend payers funding payout from earnings score near zero, and only firms actively converting the discounted hoard into shareholder cash reach the long leg, which is the specific event the agency story says should be repriced.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Dividend initiation versus omission when cheap
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), SUB(INDICATOR(dvt, 0), INDICATOR(LAG(dvt, 1), 0)))
considered.hypothesis: Among cheaply priced firms, the discrete decision to start paying a dividend is a costly, hard-to-reverse confirmation that the depressed price understates sustainable cash flow, whereas the decision to stop paying confirms that the low price is a solvency assessment — so valuation carries genuinely opposite information across the two events.
considered.reasoning: The financing leg takes values +1, 0, −1 for initiators, unchanged-status firms and omitters, so the long leg is cheap initiators and the short leg is cheap omitters — this actually tests the regime reversal that earlier conditional proposals only claimed, and it is a discrete corporate event rather than another continuous flow rescaling. Payment-status changes are not a characteristic FF5 factors are built from, dvt has near-complete panel coverage, and the design is orthogonal to the archived buyback family both in variable and in event type.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Raising equity while paying it back out
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), revt)), IND_RANK(MIN(RATIO(sstk, at), RATIO(dvt, at))))
considered.hypothesis: A firm that simultaneously sells new shares and distributes cash to existing holders is round-tripping capital at a cost; when it does so from a rich price-to-sales multiple, the issuance is opportunistic use of overvalued currency and the dividend is a signaling expense, so subsequent returns should be low.
considered.reasoning: The MIN operator identifies simultaneity — a state neither net external financing nor gross issuance can express, since netting these flows makes a raise-and-distribute firm look financially neutral — so this is not the XFIN anomaly relabeled, and it avoids gross dltis entirely and with it the revolver-rollover contamination. The financing leg is industry-ranked to prevent the signal from collapsing into a REIT and utility bet, where mandatory distribution plus continuous equity issuance is structural rather than informative, and the rich-multiple leg is on the short side where generation 1's negative sales-yield alpha says the price-multiple return actually lives.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Persistent payout mix when cheap
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(SUB(prstkc, dvt), 3), TS_SUM(ADD(prstkc, dvt), 3))))
considered.hypothesis: The instrument-choice signal reflects a standing capital-allocation policy rather than a single year's tender offer, so measuring the buyback-versus-dividend tilt over three years of cumulative payout captures the persistent managerial view of price while filtering out one-off transactions and years of accidental zero payout.
considered.reasoning: A three-year cumulation defines the mix for any firm that paid out at all in the window, which should lift coverage above the 0.079 of the single-year version and stabilize decile membership month to month — the two diagnostics most likely to be limiting the winner's alpha t-stat. It isolates a single design choice (measurement horizon of the composition variable) against the archive's best result, so the contrast is directly interpretable as noise-versus-signal in the mix leg.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Sector relative payout mix when cheap
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, dvt), ADD(prstkc, dvt))))
considered.hypothesis: Payout instrument norms are set at the industry level — utilities and staples distribute through dividends by convention while technology and healthcare distribute through repurchases — so the price-contingent decision is a firm's deviation from its own sector's payout convention, not its position in the pooled cross-section.
considered.reasoning: The pooled mix rank almost certainly contains a large static sector component that adds noise to the interaction and drags the long leg toward whole industries; ranking the mix within industry strips that component and leaves the firm-specific instrument choice the hypothesis is about. This isolates neutralization as the single varied design element against the archive's strongest result, and neutralization has already been shown to move alpha from negative to positive for the cheap-repurchaser family.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Buyback over dividend intensity when cheap
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, dvt), at)))
considered.hypothesis: If the instrument-choice effect is genuine, it should survive being expressed as a signed intensity — buyback dollars in excess of dividend dollars scaled by assets — which also assigns non-payers a well-defined score of zero rather than dropping them.
considered.reasoning: This discriminates between two very different readings of the archive's best result: a pure composition effect (bounded ratio, payers only) versus a signed magnitude effect (unbounded intensity, whole cross-section). If the intensity version reproduces the alpha, the mechanism is robust and coverage nearly doubles; if it collapses, we learn that the information is specifically in the *choice conditional on paying out*, which sharpens every subsequent refinement.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Equity versus debt retirement when cheap
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, dltr), ADD(prstkc, dltr))))
considered.hypothesis: A firm with cash to return faces a relative-value decision between retiring its own equity and retiring its own debt; choosing equity while the stock trades at a high earnings yield reveals that management judges its equity to be the cheaper claim to repurchase, whereas paying down debt at the same price reveals the opposite.
considered.reasoning: This applies the instrument-choice logic that worked to an entirely different decision margin — across the capital structure rather than between two forms of shareholder payout — so it tests whether the mechanism is "management picks the mispriced claim" or narrowly "buybacks beat dividends." Both components are uses of cash rather than a use versus a source, so the ratio is bounded and interpretable, and the cell is disjoint from the dividend-mix cell, giving genuinely incremental evidence rather than a rescaling.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Pecking order choice at a discount
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(dltis, sstk), ADD(dltis, sstk))))
considered.hypothesis: Among firms that must raise capital, the choice of instrument is the informative variable: a cheaply priced firm that funds itself with debt rather than by selling shares is refusing to issue equity it considers undervalued, while a cheaply priced firm that sells equity anyway is either constrained or aware that the discount is deserved.
considered.reasoning: This extends instrument choice to the capital-raising side, where the archive has only ever tested net or gross amounts, and it populates a completely different set of firms — issuers rather than payers — so it can raise the coverage of the mechanism family beyond the payer subsample without diluting the economics. The bounded raise-mix ratio also neutralizes firm size and financing scale, keeping the sort from degenerating into the published net-issuance anomaly.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Pure interaction of price and payout instrument
considered.expression: MUL(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, dvt), ADD(prstkc, dvt))))
considered.hypothesis: The correct instrument depends on price: retiring shares creates value when the stock is cheap and destroys it when the stock is rich, while a dividend is the neutral instrument at any price, so returns should be high for cheap buyback-tilted firms and for expensive dividend-tilted firms and low for the two mismatched cells.
considered.reasoning: Multiplying two demeaned variables produces the interaction term itself, which is approximately orthogonal to both main effects, so unlike the flagged gated version there is no mass of exact zeros, no truncated cross-section, and no residual loading on either the value premium or the payout-composition premium — a positive alpha here cannot be explained by either single-theme anomaly. This is the decisive test of whether the archive's best result is a genuine conditional mechanism or merely two additive effects riding in the same rank product, and it uses the entire payer cross-section on both sides rather than 30% of it.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Payout mix with neutral non payers
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(COALESCE(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, dvt), ADD(prstkc, dvt)), RATIO(SUB(prstkc, dvt), at))))
considered.hypothesis: A firm that distributes nothing has made no instrument choice and should be scored neutrally rather than dropped, so the payout-mix signal should extend to the full cross-section with non-payers placed between the dividend-only and buyback-only extremes.
considered.reasoning: The archive's best signal discards roughly a third of otherwise usable firm-months purely because 0/0 is undefined, and that thin, payer-only cross-section is the most likely cap on its alpha t-stat and portfolio stability. The COALESCE convention is economically justified rather than a coverage patch: when total payout is zero the fallback evaluates to exactly zero, which is precisely the neutral midpoint of the [−1, 1] mix scale, so the ordering of genuine payers is untouched while non-choosers occupy the middle.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Shift toward buybacks when cheap
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, dvt), ADD(prstkc, dvt)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: The informative act is the moment management re-weights its payout toward repurchases while the stock is cheap; a firm that has always bought back stock is executing a standing policy, whereas one that swings its mix this year is responding to a price it now considers too low.
considered.reasoning: This separates the state from the shift within the winning mechanism — an open question the archive cannot answer, since the level-based mix and the level-based net-issuance signals were tested but only net *issuance* was ever differenced. If the change version retains most of the alpha, the effect is news-driven and should be traded at higher frequency; if it collapses, the effect is a stable policy characteristic and the three-year smoothed version is the right consolidation target.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Payout mix at a composite discount
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, dvt), ADD(prstkc, dvt))))
considered.hypothesis: Whether a repurchase is value-accretive depends on true undervaluation, which a single accounting multiple measures with error — loss-makers and firms with transitory earnings are misclassified by E/P alone — so a two-multiple price signal should sharpen the same interaction.
considered.reasoning: Every instrument-choice test so far has held the valuation leg fixed at industry-ranked E/P, leaving unexamined whether the mechanism is limited by noise in the price measurement rather than in the financing measurement. Averaging the earnings and book yields before industry-ranking reduces that measurement error without changing the economic claim, and it directly addresses the negative-alpha lesson from generation 1 by keeping the price leg from being a single deep-multiple extreme.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Committed buyback tilt when cheap
considered.expression: MUL(MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, dvt), ADD(prstkc, dvt)))), RANK(RATIO(ADD(prstkc, dvt), MUL(prcc_f, csho))))
considered.hypothesis: Composition reveals the direction of management's price view and total payout yield reveals how much capital is behind it, so the strongest undervaluation evidence is a cheap firm that returns a large fraction of its market value and chooses to do so through repurchases.
considered.reasoning: The mix ratio deliberately discards magnitude, and the separate intensity test (alpha 4.2%, t=3.36) showed magnitude carries independent information, so the open question is whether the two are complementary or substitutes — a three-way rank product answers it directly. If the triple interaction beats both two-way versions, the long leg should be restricted to high-conviction, well-funded repurchasers, which is also the cell least likely to be arbitraged away by mechanical option-offset buybacks.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Payout mix against own price history
considered.expression: MUL(TS_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 5), RANK(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, dvt), ADD(prstkc, dvt))))
considered.hypothesis: The price that should govern the buyback-versus-dividend decision is the firm's own valuation relative to its history, not its rank against unrelated firms; a company tilting to repurchases while its own book-to-market sits at a five-year high is buying at its own trough.
considered.reasoning: This substitutes a within-firm price benchmark for the cross-sectional one and thereby distinguishes two very different readings of the winning result — cross-sectional value premium amplification versus genuine managerial market timing — which no archive signal has separated, since the earlier own-history test paired the trough with net repurchase *intensity* rather than with instrument choice. A within-firm benchmark also carries almost no HML loading, so a comparable alpha here would show the mechanism does not depend on riding the value factor.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Share of internal cash flow distributed when cheap
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(MUL(INDICATOR(oancf, 0), WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(prstkc, dvt), oancf), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: The prior decision to the instrument choice is what fraction of self-generated cash a firm hands back rather than retains; a cheaply priced firm that returns a large share of genuinely positive operating cash flow is resolving the agency discount on retained funds, while one that keeps it confirms the discount.
considered.reasoning: Routing the retention decision through operating cash flow rather than the change in the cash balance removes the flaw the critic identified — a firm burning cash to fund losses or capex now has no way to reach the long leg, because the INDICATOR gate zeroes out every firm with non-positive operating cash flow and the numerator counts only actual distributions rather than any decline in the cash stock. The construction keeps the scale-free, bounded character that made payout composition work, uses a 1% winsorization to stop balance-sheet-funded overdistribution from dominating the tail, and tests the retain-versus-release margin that the archive's instrument-choice results have never isolated.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Composite discount with full sample mix
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), RANK(COALESCE(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, dvt), ADD(prstkc, dvt)), RATIO(SUB(prstkc, dvt), at))))
considered.hypothesis: The instrument-choice interaction should hold on the full cross-section, with firms that distribute nothing scored at the neutral midpoint rather than excluded, so the stronger price leg and the wider sample should reinforce each other.
considered.reasoning: Coverage is the champion's one weak diagnostic (0.079), and the neutral-non-payer convention already demonstrated that widening to 0.121 costs only about one point of alpha when paired with the weaker single-multiple value leg. Pairing the wide sample with the better price measurement tests directly whether the alpha decay came from the extra firms or from noise in the E/P leg, which determines whether the deployable version of this mechanism is payer-only or universal.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Dilution adjusted payout mix at a discount
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(prstkc, sstk), dvt), ADD(ADD(prstkc, sstk), dvt))))
considered.hypothesis: A repurchase that merely absorbs shares issued to employees changes nothing about the float and reveals nothing about price, so the informative instrument choice is a distribution that shrinks the equity base net of issuance — mechanical option-offset buybacks should be stripped out before the mix is computed.
considered.reasoning: This is an economic correction rather than a rescaling: it separates firms genuinely retiring equity at a discount from firms recycling shares, a distinction the current mix ratio cannot make and one that plausibly limits the purity of the long leg. Keeping gross flows in the denominator preserves the bounded, size-neutral scale that made composition work where raw intensities did not, and a decline in performance here would itself be informative, implying the effect runs through gross distribution policy rather than through float reduction.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Mix relative to own payout policy at a discount
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), TS_RANK(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, dvt), ADD(prstkc, dvt)), 5))
considered.hypothesis: What identifies a price-contingent decision is a firm tilting toward repurchases relative to its own established payout convention, since a permanent non-dividend-payer scores at the top of the cross-sectional mix every year regardless of price while conveying no new judgment.
considered.reasoning: The cross-sectional mix level is highly persistent and therefore partly a firm type rather than a decision, while the one-year difference proved too noisy (alpha 2.5%, t=2.57, coverage collapsing to 0.065); a five-year within-firm percentile sits between these extremes and is the untested middle option. This isolates the state-versus-deviation question on the financing leg while holding the improved price leg fixed, which the archive's earlier level/change contrast could not do.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Direction of equity flow at a discount
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), ADD(prstkc, sstk))))
considered.hypothesis: The same logic that makes payout composition informative — a bounded, size-free measure of which way management chose to move — should apply to the equity market itself: conditional on transacting in its own shares at all, a cheap firm buying rather than selling reveals its price view, and this extends the mechanism to firms that issue but pay nothing out.
considered.reasoning: The archive tested net repurchase as a market-cap-scaled *intensity* (alpha 1.8%, t=1.69) but never as a bounded *direction* ratio, and the evidence across generations 2–4 is that the bounded composition form is what produces large alpha while intensity forms produce small ones. Because the denominator is gross equity activity rather than total payout, this covers dividend-free issuers and repurchasers alike, offering a route past the 0.079 payer-only coverage ceiling with an economically identical mechanism.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Buy back stock rather than assets when cheap
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, MUL(DELTA(at, 1), INDICATOR(DELTA(at, 1), 0))), ADD(prstkc, MUL(DELTA(at, 1), INDICATOR(DELTA(at, 1), 0))))))
considered.hypothesis: The deepest expression of a管理 price view is not buyback versus dividend but buyback versus expansion: a cheaply priced firm that spends its capital retiring its own shares instead of adding assets is stating that its equity is the best investment available to it, while a cheaply priced firm that expands instead is stating the opposite.
considered.reasoning: This moves the instrument-choice mechanism to a new and larger decision margin — the use of capital rather than the form of distribution — so the result cannot interpolate between two already-known outcomes the way stacked smoothing and blending knobs would. The positive-part construction on asset change repairs the defect that sank the earlier hoard design: a firm shrinking its balance sheet without repurchasing cannot reach the long leg, because the alternative use enters as zero rather than as a negative that flips the ratio, and firms doing neither are undefined rather than extreme.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Enterprise level discount with payout mix
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, dvt), ADD(prstkc, dvt))))
considered.hypothesis: Whether a repurchase is accretive depends on how the whole firm is priced, not only its equity slice: because equity is a levered claim, a given enterprise-level discount translates into a much larger per-share gain for a levered firm, so the enterprise multiple is the economically correct price benchmark for the buyback decision.
considered.reasoning: This replaces rather than augments the price leg, so it is not a third correlated equity multiple layered onto two existing ones — it tests a different economic claim about which price management is transacting against, and it corrects the systematic misranking of levered value firms by E/P and B/M. The denominator adds debt to market capitalization without subtracting cash, so it is strictly positive and free of the sign-flip failure that made net-cash firms uninterpretable in the earlier enterprise-value attempt.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Net debt enterprise discount with payout mix
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), SUB(ADD(dltt, dlc), MIN(che, ADD(dltt, dlc)))))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, dvt), ADD(prstkc, dvt))))
considered.hypothesis: Cash on the balance sheet is not part of the price of the operating business and is precisely what funds a repurchase, so the enterprise discount that governs buyback accretion should be measured net of cash — a cash-rich firm buying back stock is cheaper than its gross enterprise multiple suggests.
considered.reasoning: This repairs the flaw that disqualified the generation-0 enterprise-value attempt — subtracting cash outright can drive the denominator negative and invert the ranking for exactly the net-cash firms the mechanism cares about — by capping the cash subtraction at total debt via MIN, so net debt is floored at zero and the denominator can never fall below market capitalization. It isolates one economically meaningful change to the best-slope price leg, and cash-funded repurchases are the modal case in the long leg, so the correction should bite where it matters.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cyclically adjusted discount with payout mix
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(MA(ib, 3), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, dvt), ADD(prstkc, dvt))))
considered.hypothesis: Management judges its price against normalized earning power, not against one year's reported income, so a three-year average earnings yield is the price benchmark that actually governs the repurchase decision and should classify cyclical troughs and one-off charges correctly.
considered.reasoning: The price-leg upgrades that worked so far attacked cross-sectional measurement error by blending multiples; this attacks time-series measurement error in the same variable, a distinct and untested source of noise that is largest exactly where the mechanism lives — cheap, cyclical, cash-generating repurchasers whose current-year earnings understate normal profitability. It also keeps the single-multiple simplicity and full E/P coverage rather than adding correlated proxies.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cheapest claim to retire at a firm level discount
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, dltr), ADD(prstkc, dltr))))
considered.hypothesis: The choice between retiring equity and retiring debt is a relative-value judgment about two claims on the same enterprise, so it should be evaluated against the price of the enterprise rather than against the price of the equity alone.
considered.reasoning: This margin produced only a modest result (alpha 2.0%, t=1.84) when paired with an equity earnings yield, but that pairing was conceptually mismatched — a decision about which claim to buy back is meaningful only relative to how the whole firm is priced, which is exactly what the enterprise multiple measures. It is the one alternative decision margin whose earlier weakness is plausibly attributable to the price leg rather than to the financing construct, so it is worth one slot before the mechanism is finalized.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Self funded buyback tilt at a firm level discount
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(MUL(INDICATOR(oancf, 0), MIN(prstkc, oancf)), dvt), ADD(MUL(INDICATOR(oancf, 0), MIN(prstkc, oancf)), dvt))))
considered.hypothesis: A repurchase paid for out of the year's own operating cash flow is a statement about price, whereas one paid for by borrowing is primarily a capital-structure decision, so the price-revealing instrument choice is the buyback tilt computed only on the self-funded portion of repurchases.
